title: Don't bother patching: multiple remote code execution vulnerabilities in Danfoss AK-SM800A
excerpt: Following up on the waves of cyber attacks against internet-exposed fridge controllers, this blogpost argues to not waste time patching vulnerabilities on these devices by showing how we found several pre-authentication remote code execution 0-day vulnerabilities in the Danfoss AK-SM 800A in less than an hour with casual manual inspection. Instead, we recommend prioritizing reducing exposure.
content_html:
Background

Prior to the attack waves which started in France on October 11th, several vulnerabilities had already been documented in multiple Danfoss product lines (AK SM-800, AK SM-800A, AK-EM100) by SynAcktiv (in 2023 [1,2]), Claroty (in 2025 [3]), and DIVD/HackDefense (in 2023 [4]).

These vulnerabilities have included the much-discussed code-of-the-day authentication bypass (CVE-2025-41450), OS command injection (CVE-2023-25915, CVE-2025-41451) and path traversal (CVE-2023-25914) vulnerabilities in the AK-SM800A, as well as SQL injection (CVE-2023-22583) and OS command injection (CVE-2023-25911) vulnerabilities in the EOL AK-EM100.

All of these vulnerabilities are shockingly trivial to find and exploit, and the first public Proof-of-Concept (PoC) exploits were dropped within 48 hours of the French attacks [5, 6] - preceding the second attack wave on November 2nd.

According to Censys, there are still hundreds of Danfoss systems exposed online (though no doubt a sizeable chunk are by now honeypots) and over a 1000 Copeland and Dixell fridge controllers. In addition, controllers from similar vendors (such as Eliwell) which have not been targeted remain exposed in the hundreds as well.

‍

All this is to say that despite the demonstrable subpar security posture of these controllers and several attack waves with serious impact, controllers remain exposed to the public internet. While this is for understandable reasons (supermarket chains sometimes risk SLA or insurance condition violations by taking away remote maintenance and restricting access through VPNs isn't a trivial systems change), we consider it of paramount importance for defenders not to fall into the trap of considering risks sufficiently mitigated by applying patches as is suggested by Danfoss guidance.

In order to demonstrate this, we investigated the latest Danfoss AK-SM800A firmware version (5.3.2 at the time of writing) and within an hour of manual investigation (no AI necessary...) uncovered 6 pre-authentication remote code execution 0-day vulnerabilities.

‍

We are currently in a coordinated vulnerability disclosure process with Danfoss and as such will withhold technical details until disclosure is sorted, but due to ongoing targeting of these controllers we consider it important asset owners have a realistic view of the overall security posture of these devices ontrollers in order to take the appropriate measures rather than rely on piecemeal patching.

‍

Overview

  • CVEs: Pending
  • ‍Vendor: Danfoss
  • Affected products: AK-SM800A
  • Affected versions: All up to and including 5.3.2
  • Vulnerability type: Multiple (6) stack-based buffer overflows
  • ‍Potential impact: Full device take-over, Persistent access (possibly after reset), Persistent Denial of Service (rendering device inoperable)

  • Mitigation: Restrict network exposure through VPNs, private APN, or highly restrictive IP whitelisting ACLs

‍

60 minutes and a firmware image

Initial Investigation & Setup

Danfoss AK-SM800A firmware images can be downloaded from their website and contain 7-zip compressed ARM binaries handling application logic. Danfoss AK-SM800A controllers run Danux, a custom Yocto-based Linux distribution, on an i.MX6 processor.

Let's start by setting up an emulation environment for the firmware. The path of least resistance here is emulating the binary in userland, rather than emulating the entire system including the kernel. After mounting the filesystem, we can copy qemu-armel-static in there and run the following command to be presented with a shell:

$ sudo chroot . /qemu-armel-static /bin/sh
sh-4.4#

‍

As pointed out by Claroty, the SM800A platform consists of an NGINX reverse proxy, a bunch of CGI handlers, and independent processes handling application logic. Requests for URLs ending with .cgi suffix are forwarded to a task created by the sm_app executable.

It turns out that sm_app is a huge monolithic application that is responsible for pretty much everything that happens on the device. It is more like a mini Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) running in a userland process (a common embedded architectural choice resulting from lift-and-shift platform migrations). It has a task (thread) list consisting of 52 entries, among which are Task_Modbus_drv_task, Task_Ethernet, Task_IOHandler and Task_Web to name a few. Running the sm_app in this environment that's missing a significant chunk of the devices and drivers will almost certainly end in a crash. Applying some ad-hoc patches to the binary to avoid crashes will probably work, but potentially painful.

Fortunately, we're only interested in Task_Web, so instead of fixing up everything, I can just LD_PRELOAD my way in the binary, let it run all the initialization code until it hits main(), hijack the code flow from there, apply some hooks which I won't delve into here, and start the web server. It turns out that Danux conveniently ships with gcc:

$ gcc -shared -g -fPIC -o libpreload.so preload.c
$ sudo chroot . /qemu-armel-static -E LD_PRELOAD=/libpreload3.so /danfoss/sm_app
hi from hijacked code

‍

With some additional minor fixes, we are now able to talk to the emulated web server:

Worrying Code Smells

The first thing to do is get a sense of the security quality of the code base through so-called code smells and anti-patterns.

The first such bad code smell is the extremely liberal use of strcpy. Use of the strcpy() function is discouraged as there is no size parameter. Instead, the function will keep copying bytes from the source buffer into the destination until it hits a null byte. This is a common source of memory corruption vulnerabilities in cases where the source buffer is provided by the user. Hundreds of strcpy invocations exist in the codebase which are part of externally reachable and unauthenticated handler functions. In fact, in earlier firmware releases each command handler is itself responsible for enforcing authentication, rather than doing so centrally. This needlessly enlarged the pre-authentication attack surface.

‍

Next, we check for binary security mechanisms and exploit mitigations:

$ checksec sm_app
[*] '/mnt/SM800A-4.2.4/sm_app'
    Arch:     arm-32-little
    RELRO:    Partial RELRO
    Stack:    No canary found
    NX:       NX enabled
    PIE:      No PIE (0x10000)
    RPATH:    b'$ORIGIN:$ORIGIN/../../sm_gp_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_fu_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_df_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_msgqueue_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_lz_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_tm_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_up_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_history_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_thread_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_fs_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_at_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_mutex_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_lg_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_system_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_os_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_ip_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_dl_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_db_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_tk_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_session_lib/Debug/'

‍

It turns out that stack canaries and Position Independent Executable (PIE) are not enabled. These mechanisms have been staples of memory corruption defenses for decades and enabling these features on a modern Linux distribution running on a modern ARM application processor requires no engineering work at all. It is simply a matter of setting the right compiler flag. Enabling these features became the default in Ubuntu 17.10 and there is simply no excuse for a network-facing application that was last updated a few months ago to not have them enabled.

What's more worrying, is that multiple Danfoss business units (including Climate Solutions & Electronic Controllers) received IEC 62443-4-1 certification for Secure Product Development Lifecycle and this is prominently advertised as such. In addition, Danfoss explicitly mentions IEC 62443-4-2 is a guiding framework for designing cybersecurity requirements and implementing improvements. Asset owners, system integrators, and those responsible for procurement should realize exactly how little such certifications can say about the actual security posture of a product.

‍

‍

Vulnerability Discovery & PoC Development

The initial impression of Danfoss' security posture, combined with the nature of the historical vulnerabilities, is a worrying one. But to see just how bad this pans out, let's see what can be found in no more than one hour of manually digging through the latest version of the firmware.

We could develop a harness and subject the binary to coverage-guided fuzzing. However, that constitutes serious effort, and with the impression of the code quality that I have, I'm going to simply look into random places where strcpy() is invoked instead. One of the first functions inspected turns out to be an unauthenticated endpoint for a CGI handler having a bunch of parsing logic and strcpy invocations.

While we will not disclose the exact endpoint affected, we will show it can be trivially exploited with a oneliner:

$ curl -v -d <redacted>"$(echo 'print("A"*768)'|python)"<redacted> http://127.0.0.1:8080/<redacted>.cgi
*   Trying 127.0.0.1:8080...
* Connected to 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.1) port 8080
> POST /<redacted>.cgi HTTP/1.1
> Host: 127.0.0.1:8080
> User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
> Accept: */*
> Content-Length: 888
> Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
>

‍

This gives us a nice SEGFAULT showing we can probably hijack program control flow:

‍

There's at least 5 different vulnerabilities of this kind in just the little bit of code i inspected.

Of course, remotely triggering a crash is bad in itself, but being able to leverage the buffer overflow to obtain remote code execution is much worse. Any reasonably experienced exploit developer will agree exploiting straightforward stack-based buffer overflows on ARM Linux without exploit mitigations is very straightforward. And if they don't, there's probably a frontier or open weight model out there willing to help them agree.

The only challenge (if you can call it that) left to overcome is the fact that strcpy() stops copying bytes when it hits a null byte. If we wish to gain remote code execution, we inevitably need to write several addresses containing null bytes. Thus, we need to somehow overcome this inherent limitation of strcpy() and while we won't share our approach for now it's not exactly rocket surgery. Also, the exploited application runs as root (because of course it does).

Danfoss Security Levels & Strict Mode

The exploit demonstrated above was targeted at version 3.3.0, but the bugs are present in the latest version of the firmware as well (5.3.2 at the time of writing).

In later firmware versions, however, the concepts of session control and security levels were introduced by Danfoss [1,2]. According to Danfoss, session control is an authentication rules engine for the various remote interfaces (StoreView Browser, StoreView Web, Alsense, and 3rd party XML). This session control mechanism replaces the individual handler-level authentication enforcement mentioned above.

Session control has three security levels: backward compatible, permissive, and strict. Starting at 4.0 security level strict was set as the default which:

  • Enforces HTTPS
  • 3rd party XML requests cannot contain usernames and passwords and session tokens must be provided in the AKSM-auth header

This AKSM-auth header mechanism historically held a base64 encoded username and password as the authentication key but now needs to include a session token derived from initial authentication [3]. At the strict security level, virtually all the web-accessible attack surface is fenced off from unauthenticated users (including the bug that was used in the exploit above) which is why enabling this security control was included in CERT-FR's official mitigations.

Unfortunately, it turns out the session control mechanism also has at least one trivial pre-authentication memory corruption vulnerability.

The way this is implemented is through a separate binary: sm_fcgi_app. It acts as a Web Application Firewall (WAF) in the sense that it passes through all commands to NGINX if it believes that the user is authenticated. If not, then the only command allowed to be passed through is the getauth command, which is used to authenticate.

At first glance i spotted a potential for parser differential attacks on sm_fcgi_app which might open the entire attack surface to unauthenticated users, but decided to investigate a quicker route to success. It turns out there's another simple strcpy based pre-authentication memory corruption:

‍

$ curl -k -v -d <redacted> -A "$(echo 'print("A"*1536)'|python)" https://127.0.0.1:3443/<redacted>.cgi
...
> POST /<redacted>.cgi HTTP/1.1
> Host: 127.0.0.1:3443
> User-Agent: AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA...AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA
> Accept: */*
> Content-Length: 41
> Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
>

‍

Running this against the latest AK-SM800A firmware with strict session control enabled produces a SEGFAULT which, with some additional effort, can be turned into yet another pre-authentication RCE. It goes without saying that sm_fcgi_app does not have stack canaries and PIE enabled either. I think we're done here, we've seen enough.

‍

Persistence and Bricking Risks

The last thing we want to figure out is exactly how bad this can get.

It's one thing to initiate long defrost cycles and spoil tens of millions of food once, but the typical response of defenders is to factory reset affected controllers, rotate credentials, apply patches, set strict session control mode, and possibly wall off the controllers from internet exposure. But any controllers that are hit continue to do their job in production.

Now, imagine an attacker who manages to persist on such controllers. They don't just trigger the initial payload but they leave a little implant that survives a factory reset and firmware update. With OS level access, this isn't too hard on typical Unix-like devices as shown in the SALTWATER / SEASPY malware for Barracuda devices, FIRESTARTER malware for Cisco devices, and Sonicwall malware all which survive firmware updates.

In such a scenario, an attacker could either retain remote access or leave a time-triggered payload for a 2nd (or 3rd...) strike - increasing damage by spoiling new batches of food. Alternatively, attackers could simply wipe flash memory and/or push a malformed firmware update to brick the controllers and render them permanently inoperable - requiring costly and time-consuming replacement similar to the TTPs deployed during the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid.

Both approaches seem feasible against the AK-SM800A controllers since they do not make use of the i.MX6's secure boot features as evidenced by checking some of the responsible One-Time Programmable (OTP) fuse registers.

‍

Potential impact

1. Full device take-over: Through remote code execution, an unauthenticated attacker can remotely run arbitrary code at the operating system level of the AK-SM800A controller. This would allow the attacker to change parameters or initiate unwanted actions (such as defrosting operations) while hiding their activities from any system logs. In addition, the lack of secure boot functionality would allow an attacker with RCE to persistently implant controllers to maintain access or have it trigger a secondary payload at a later point in time. Without deep introspection and forensics capabilities, determining whether a device is implanted at the firmware level (even after a factory reset) is infeasible.

‍

2. Equipment damage (bricking): Due to the lack of secure boot, an attacker with RCE could push malicious firmware that simply renders the device inoperable and irrecoverable without specialized hardware intervention (e.g. by wiping flash memory and/or causing an infinite boot loop). Such a 'bricking' or wiper approach would require full device replacement. The dangers of such a scenario to OT equipment in particular and adversary deployment of such TTPs have been highlighted in previous blogposts by Midnight Blue [1,2]. This could potentially lead to freezers being unavailable for days or longer while controllers get replaced.

‍

Mitigations

In light of all of the above, we consider piecemeal patching or enabling of strict session control to be a misallocation of scarce security and personnel resources since they have minimal security ROI against such a fundamentally flawed codebase missing basic exploit mitigations and yielding multiple pre-auth RCEs with an hour's casual glance.

Instead, we strongly recommend asset owners and system integrators to take the following course of action for all Danfoss, Copeland, and Dixell controllers and preferably for similar controllers by other vendors as well:

  1. Inventarise which controllers are internet exposed, not just on asset owner public IP ranges but also through system integrator 4G modems
    ‍
  2. Ensure controller management interfaces are only accessible through either a VPN, a private APN, or highly restrictive firewall-enforced IP whitelist (broad IP geofencing or blacklisting is not sufficient). As per CERT-FR recommendations, IP whitelisting is an intermediate mitigation and not long-term sustainable due to the risk of configuration drift and change management challenges.

At the strict security level, virtually all the web-accessible attack surface is fenced off from unauthenticated users (including the bug that was used in the exploit above) which is why enabling this security control was included in CERT-FR's official mitigations.Unfortunately, it turns out the session control mechanism also has at least one trivial pre-authentication memory corruption vulnerability.The way this is implemented is through a separate binary: sm_fcgi_app. It acts as a Web Application Firewall (WAF) in the sense that it passes through all commands to NGINX if it believes that the user is authenticated. If not, then the only command allowed to be passed through is the getauth command, which is used to authenticate.At first glance i spotted a potential for parser differential attacks on sm_fcgi_app which might open the entire attack surface to unauthenticated users, but decided to investigate a quicker route to success. It turns out there's another simple strcpy based pre-authentication memory corruption:‍$ curl -k -v -d <redacted> -A "$(echo 'print("A"*1536)'|python)" https://127.0.0.1:3443/<redacted>.cgi ... > POST /<redacted>.cgi HTTP/1.1 > Host: 127.0.0.1:3443 > User-Agent: AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA...AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA > Accept: */* > Content-Length: 41 > Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded > ‍Running this against the latest AK-SM800A firmware with strict session control enabled produces a SEGFAULT which, with some additional effort, can be turned into yet another pre-authentication RCE. It goes without saying that sm_fcgi_app does not have stack canaries and PIE enabled either. I think we're done here, we've seen enough.‍Persistence and Bricking RisksThe last thing we want to figure out is exactly how bad this can get.It's one thing to initiate long defrost cycles and spoil tens of millions of food once, but the typical response of defenders is to factory reset affected controllers, rotate credentials, apply patches, set strict session control mode, and possibly wall off the controllers from internet exposure. But any controllers that are hit continue to do their job in production.Now, imagine an attacker who manages to persist on such controllers. They don't just trigger the initial payload but they leave a little implant that survives a factory reset and firmware update. With OS level access, this isn't too hard on typical Unix-like devices as shown in the SALTWATER / SEASPY malware for Barracuda devices, FIRESTARTER malware for Cisco devices, and Sonicwall malware all which survive firmware updates.In such a scenario, an attacker could either retain remote access or leave a time-triggered payload for a 2nd (or 3rd...) strike - increasing damage by spoiling new batches of food. Alternatively, attackers could simply wipe flash memory and/or push a malformed firmware update to brick the controllers and render them permanently inoperable - requiring costly and time-consuming replacement similar to the TTPs deployed during the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid.Both approaches seem feasible against the AK-SM800A controllers since they do not make use of the i.MX6's secure boot features as evidenced by checking some of the responsible One-Time Programmable (OTP) fuse registers.‍Potential impact1. Full device take-over: Through remote code execution, an unauthenticated attacker can remotely run arbitrary code at the operating system level of the AK-SM800A controller. This would allow the attacker to change parameters or initiate unwanted actions (such as defrosting operations) while hiding their activities from any system logs. In addition, the lack of secure boot functionality would allow an attacker with RCE to persistently implant controllers to maintain access or have it trigger a secondary payload at a later point in time. Without deep introspection and forensics capabilities, determining whether a device is implanted at the firmware level (even after a factory reset) is infeasible.‍2. Equipment damage (bricking): Due to the lack of secure boot, an attacker with RCE could push malicious firmware that simply renders the device inoperable and irrecoverable without specialized hardware intervention (e.g. by wiping flash memory and/or causing an infinite boot loop). Such a 'bricking' or wiper approach would require full device replacement. The dangers of such a scenario to OT equipment in particular and adversary deployment of such TTPs have been highlighted in previous blogposts by Midnight Blue [1,2]. This could potentially lead to freezers being unavailable for days or longer while controllers get replaced.‍MitigationsIn light of all of the above, we consider piecemeal patching or enabling of strict session control to be a misallocation of scarce security and personnel resources since they have minimal security ROI against such a fundamentally flawed codebase missing basic exploit mitigations and yielding multiple pre-auth RCEs with an hour's casual glance.Instead, we strongly recommend asset owners and system integrators to take the following course of action for all Danfoss, Copeland, and Dixell controllers and preferably for similar controllers by other vendors as well:Inventarise which controllers are internet exposed, not just on asset owner public IP ranges but also through system integrator 4G modems‍Ensure controller management interfaces are only accessible through either a VPN, a private APN, or highly restrictive firewall-enforced IP whitelist (broad IP geofencing or blacklisting is not sufficient). As per CERT-FR recommendations, IP whitelisting is an intermediate mitigation and not long-term sustainable due to the risk of configuration drift and change management challenges.‍

content_html_zh:
背景

Prior to the attack waves which started in France on October 11th, several vulnerabilities had already been documented in multiple Danfoss product lines (AK SM-800, AK SM-800A, AK-EM100) by SynAcktiv (in 2023 [1,2]), Claroty (in 2025 [3]), and DIVD/HackDefense (in 2023 [4]).

These vulnerabilities have included the much-discussed code-of-the-day authentication bypass (CVE-2025-41450), OS command injection (CVE-2023-25915, CVE-2025-41451) and path traversal (CVE-2023-25914) vulnerabilities in the AK-SM800A, as well as SQL injection (CVE-2023-22583) and OS command injection (CVE-2023-25911) vulnerabilities in the EOL AK-EM100.

All of these vulnerabilities are shockingly trivial to find and exploit, and the first public Proof-of-Concept (PoC) exploits were dropped within 48 hours of the French attacks [5, 6] - preceding the second attack wave on November 2nd.

According to Censys, there are still hundreds of Danfoss systems exposed online (though no doubt a sizeable chunk are by now honeypots) and over a 1000 Copeland and Dixell fridge controllers. In addition, controllers from similar vendors (such as Eliwell) which have not been targeted remain exposed in the hundreds as well.

‍

All this is to say that despite the demonstrable subpar security posture of these controllers and several attack waves with serious impact, controllers remain exposed to the public internet. While this is for understandable reasons (supermarket chains sometimes risk SLA or insurance condition violations by taking away remote maintenance and restricting access through VPNs isn't a trivial systems change), we consider it of paramount importance for defenders not to fall into the trap of considering risks sufficiently mitigated by applying patches as is suggested by Danfoss guidance.

In order to demonstrate this, we investigated the latest Danfoss AK-SM800A firmware version (5.3.2 at the time of writing) and within an hour of manual investigation (no AI necessary...) uncovered 6 pre-authentication remote code execution 0-day vulnerabilities.

‍

We are currently in a coordinated vulnerability disclosure process with Danfoss and as such will withhold technical details until disclosure is sorted, but due to ongoing targeting of these controllers we consider it important asset owners have a realistic view of the overall security posture of these devices ontrollers in order to take the appropriate measures rather than rely on piecemeal patching.

‍

概述

  • CVEs: Pending
  • ‍Vendor: Danfoss
  • Affected products: AK-SM800A
  • Affected versions: All up to and including 5.3.2
  • Vulnerability type: Multiple (6) stack-based buffer overflows
  • ‍Potential impact: Full device take-over, Persistent access (possibly after reset), Persistent Denial of Service (rendering device inoperable)
  • Mitigation: Restrict network exposure through VPNs, private APN, or highly restrictive IP whitelisting ACLs

‍

60 minutes and a firmware image

Initial Investigation & Setup

Danfoss AK-SM800A firmware images can be downloaded from their website and contain 7-zip compressed ARM binaries handling application logic. Danfoss AK-SM800A controllers run Danux, a custom Yocto-based Linux distribution, on an i.MX6 processor.

Let's start by setting up an emulation environment for the firmware. The path of least resistance here is emulating the binary in userland, rather than emulating the entire system including the kernel. After mounting the filesystem, we can copy qemu-armel-static in there and run the following command to be presented with a shell:

$ sudo chroot . /qemu-armel-static /bin/sh
sh-4.4#

‍

As pointed out by Claroty, the SM800A platform consists of an NGINX reverse proxy, a bunch of CGI handlers, and independent processes handling application logic. Requests for URLs ending with .cgi suffix are forwarded to a task created by the sm_app executable.

It turns out that sm_app is a huge monolithic application that is responsible for pretty much everything that happens on the device. It is more like a mini Real-Time Operating System (RTOS) running in a userland process (a common embedded architectural choice resulting from lift-and-shift platform migrations). It has a task (thread) list consisting of 52 entries, among which are Task_Modbus_drv_task, Task_Ethernet, Task_IOHandler and Task_Web to name a few. Running the sm_app in this environment that's missing a significant chunk of the devices and drivers will almost certainly end in a crash. Applying some ad-hoc patches to the binary to avoid crashes will probably work, but potentially painful.

Fortunately, we're only interested in Task_Web, so instead of fixing up everything, I can just LD_PRELOAD my way in the binary, let it run all the initialization code until it hits main(), hijack the code flow from there, apply some hooks which I won't delve into here, and start the web server. It turns out that Danux conveniently ships with gcc:

$ gcc -shared -g -fPIC -o libpreload.so preload.c
$ sudo chroot . /qemu-armel-static -E LD_PRELOAD=/libpreload3.so /danfoss/sm_app
hi from hijacked code

‍

With some additional minor fixes, we are now able to talk to the emulated web server:

$ curl -v -d '' http://127.0.0.1:8080/xml.cgi

‍

Worrying Code Smells

The first thing to do is get a sense of the security quality of the code base through so-called code smells and anti-patterns.

The first such bad code smell is the extremely liberal use of strcpy. Use of the strcpy() function is discouraged as there is no size parameter. Instead, the function will keep copying bytes from the source buffer into the destination until it hits a null byte. This is a common source of memory corruption vulnerabilities in cases where the source buffer is provided by the user. Hundreds of strcpy invocations exist in the codebase which are part of externally reachable and unauthenticated handler functions. In fact, in earlier firmware releases each command handler is itself responsible for enforcing authentication, rather than doing so centrally. This needlessly enlarged the pre-authentication attack surface.

‍

Next, we check for binary security mechanisms and exploit mitigations:

$ checksec sm_app
[*] '/mnt/SM800A-4.2.4/sm_app'
    Arch:     arm-32-little
    RELRO:    Partial RELRO
    Stack:    No canary found
    NX:       NX enabled
    PIE:      No PIE (0x10000)
    RPATH:    b'$ORIGIN:$ORIGIN/../../sm_gp_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_fu_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_df_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_msgqueue_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_lz_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_tm_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_up_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_history_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_thread_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_fs_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_at_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_mutex_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_lg_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_system_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_os_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_ip_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_dl_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_db_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_tk_lib/Debug/:$ORIGIN/../../sm_session_lib/Debug/'

‍

It turns out that stack canaries and Position Independent Executable (PIE) are not enabled. These mechanisms have been staples of memory corruption defenses for decades and enabling these features on a modern Linux distribution running on a modern ARM application processor requires no engineering work at all. It is simply a matter of setting the right compiler flag. Enabling these features became the default in Ubuntu 17.10 and there is simply no excuse for a network-facing application that was last updated a few months ago to not have them enabled.

What's more worrying, is that multiple Danfoss business units (including Climate Solutions & Electronic Controllers) received IEC 62443-4-1 certification for Secure Product Development Lifecycle and this is prominently advertised as such. In addition, Danfoss explicitly mentions IEC 62443-4-2 is a guiding framework for designing cybersecurity requirements and implementing improvements. Asset owners, system integrators, and those responsible for procurement should realize exactly how little such certifications can say about the actual security posture of a product.

‍

‍

Vulnerability Discovery & PoC Development

The initial impression of Danfoss' security posture, combined with the nature of the historical vulnerabilities, is a worrying one. But to see just how bad this pans out, let's see what can be found in no more than one hour of manually digging through the latest version of the firmware.

We could develop a harness and subject the binary to coverage-guided fuzzing. However, that constitutes serious effort, and with the impression of the code quality that I have, I'm going to simply look into random places where strcpy() is invoked instead. One of the first functions inspected turns out to be an unauthenticated endpoint for a CGI handler having a bunch of parsing logic and strcpy invocations.

While we will not disclose the exact endpoint affected, we will show it can be trivially exploited with a oneliner:

$ curl -v -d <redacted>"$(echo 'print("A"*768)'|python)"<redacted> http://127.0.0.1:8080/<redacted>.cgi
*   Trying 127.0.0.1:8080...
* Connected to 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.1) port 8080
> POST /<redacted>.cgi HTTP/1.1
> Host: 127.0.0.1:8080
> User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
> Accept: */*
> Content-Length: 888
> Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
>

‍

This gives us a nice SEGFAULT showing we can probably hijack program control flow:

‍

There's at least 5 different vulnerabilities of this kind in just the little bit of code i inspected.

Of course, remotely triggering a crash is bad in itself, but being able to leverage the buffer overflow to obtain remote code execution is much worse. Any reasonably experienced exploit developer will agree exploiting straightforward stack-based buffer overflows on ARM Linux without exploit mitigations is very straightforward. And if they don't, there's probably a frontier or open weight model out there willing to help them agree.

The only challenge (if you can call it that) left to overcome is the fact that strcpy() stops copying bytes when it hits a null byte. If we wish to gain remote code execution, we inevitably need to write several addresses containing null bytes. Thus, we need to somehow overcome this inherent limitation of strcpy() and while we won't share our approach for now it's not exactly rocket surgery. Also, the exploited application runs as root (because of course it does).

Danfoss Security Levels & Strict Mode

The exploit demonstrated above was targeted at version 3.3.0, but the bugs are present in the latest version of the firmware as well (5.3.2 at the time of writing).

In later firmware versions, however, the concepts of session control and security levels were introduced by Danfoss [1,2]. According to Danfoss, session control is an authentication rules engine for the various remote interfaces (StoreView Browser, StoreView Web, Alsense, and 3rd party XML). This session control mechanism replaces the individual handler-level authentication enforcement mentioned above.

Session control has three security levels: backward compatible, permissive, and strict. Starting at 4.0 security level strict was set as the default which:

  • Enforces HTTPS
  • 3rd party XML requests cannot contain usernames and passwords and session tokens must be provided in the AKSM-auth header

This AKSM-auth header mechanism historically held a base64 encoded username and password as the authentication key but now needs to include a session token derived from initial authentication [3]. At the strict security level, virtually all the web-accessible attack surface is fenced off from unauthenticated users (including the bug that was used in the exploit above) which is why enabling this security control was included in CERT-FR's official mitigations.

Unfortunately, it turns out the session control mechanism also has at least one trivial pre-authentication memory corruption vulnerability.

The way this is implemented is through a separate binary: sm_fcgi_app. It acts as a Web Application Firewall (WAF) in the sense that it passes through all commands to NGINX if it believes that the user is authenticated. If not, then the only command allowed to be passed through is the getauth command, which is used to authenticate.

At first glance i spotted a potential for parser differential attacks on sm_fcgi_app which might open the entire attack surface to unauthenticated users, but decided to investigate a quicker route to success. It turns out there's another simple strcpy based pre-authentication memory corruption:

‍

$ curl -k -v -d <redacted> -A "$(echo 'print("A"*1536)'|python)" https://127.0.0.1:3443/<redacted>.cgi
...
> POST /<redacted>.cgi HTTP/1.1
> Host: 127.0.0.1:3443
> User-Agent: AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA...AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA
> Accept: */*
> Content-Length: 41
> Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
>

‍

Running this against the latest AK-SM800A firmware with strict session control enabled produces a SEGFAULT which, with some additional effort, can be turned into yet another pre-authentication RCE. It goes without saying that sm_fcgi_app does not have stack canaries and PIE enabled either. I think we're done here, we've seen enough.

‍

Persistence and Bricking Risks

The last thing we want to figure out is exactly how bad this can get.

It's one thing to initiate long defrost cycles and spoil tens of millions of food once, but the typical response of defenders is to factory reset affected controllers, rotate credentials, apply patches, set strict session control mode, and possibly wall off the controllers from internet exposure. But any controllers that are hit continue to do their job in production.

Now, imagine an attacker who manages to persist on such controllers. They don't just trigger the initial payload but they leave a little implant that survives a factory reset and firmware update. With OS level access, this isn't too hard on typical Unix-like devices as shown in the SALTWATER / SEASPY malware for Barracuda devices, FIRESTARTER malware for Cisco devices, and Sonicwall malware all which survive firmware updates.

In such a scenario, an attacker could either retain remote access or leave a time-triggered payload for a 2nd (or 3rd...) strike - increasing damage by spoiling new batches of food. Alternatively, attackers could simply wipe flash memory and/or push a malformed firmware update to brick the controllers and render them permanently inoperable - requiring costly and time-consuming replacement similar to the TTPs deployed during the December 2025 attack on the Polish electric grid.

Both approaches seem feasible against the AK-SM800A controllers since they do not make use of the i.MX6's secure boot features as evidenced by checking some of the responsible One-Time Programmable (OTP) fuse registers.

‍

Potential impact

1. Full device take-over: Through remote code execution, an unauthenticated attacker can remotely run arbitrary code at the operating system level of the AK-SM800A controller. This would allow the attacker to change parameters or initiate unwanted actions (such as defrosting operations) while hiding their activities from any system logs. In addition, the lack of secure boot functionality would allow an attacker with RCE to persistently implant controllers to maintain access or have it trigger a secondary payload at a later point in time. Without deep introspection and forensics capabilities, determining whether a device is implanted at the firmware level (even after a factory reset) is infeasible.

‍

2. Equipment damage (bricking): Due to the lack of secure boot, an attacker with RCE could push malicious firmware that simply renders the device inoperable and irrecoverable without specialized hardware intervention (e.g. by wiping flash memory and/or causing an infinite boot loop). Such a 'bricking' or wiper approach would require full device replacement. The dangers of such a scenario to OT equipment in particular and adversary deployment of such TTPs have been highlighted in previous blogposts by Midnight Blue [1,2]. This could potentially lead to freezers being unavailable for days or longer while controllers get replaced.

‍

缓解措施

In light of all of the above, we consider piecemeal patching or enabling of strict session control to be a misallocation of scarce security and personnel resources since they have minimal security ROI against such a fundamentally flawed codebase missing basic exploit mitigations and yielding multiple pre-auth RCEs with an hour's casual glance.

Instead, we strongly recommend asset owners and system integrators to take the following course of action for all Danfoss, Copeland, and Dixell controllers and preferably for similar controllers by other vendors as well:

  1. Inventarise which controllers are internet exposed, not just on asset owner public IP ranges but also through system integrator 4G modems‍
  2. Ensure controller management interfaces are only accessible through either a VPN, a private APN, or highly restrictive firewall-enforced IP whitelist (broad IP geofencing or blacklisting is not sufficient). As per CERT-FR recommendations, IP whitelisting is an intermediate mitigation and not long-term sustainable due to the risk of configuration drift and change management challenges.
